Department of Microbiology, Immunology and Molecular Genetics University of California, Los Angeles Los Angeles United States † Corresponding author ## Abstract Aminoacyl-tRNA synthetases use a variety of mechanisms to ensure fidelity of the genetic code and ultimately select the correct amino acids to be used in protein synthesis. The physiological necessity of these quality control mechanisms in different environments remains unclear, as the cost vs benefit of accurate protein synthesis is difficult to predict. We show that in Escherichia coli, a non-coded amino acid produced through oxidative damage is a significant threat to the accuracy of protein synthesis and must be cleared by phenylalanine-tRNA synthetase in order to prevent cellular toxicity caused by mis-synthesized proteins. These findings demonstrate how stress can lead to the accumulation of non-canonical amino acids that must be excluded from the proteome in order to maintain cellular viability. ## Introduction The faithful translation of mRNA into the corresponding protein sequence is an essential step in gene expression. The accuracy of translation depends on the precise pairing of mRNA codons with their cognate aminoacyl-tRNAs, containing the corresponding anticodons, during ribosomal protein synthesis (Zaher and Green, 2009; Rodnina, 2012). Cognate amino acids are attached to their respective tRNAs by aminoacyl-tRNA synthetases (aaRSs), and the ability of these enzymes to distinguish between cognate and non-cognate substrates is a major determinant of the fidelity of the genetic code. AaRSs discriminate against near- and non-cognate tRNAs at levels compatible with typical translation error rates (∼10−4) due to the structural complexity and diversity observed between tRNA isoacceptors. AaRSs can less successfully discriminate against near-cognate amino acids, which may differ from the cognate substrate by as little as a single methyl or hydroxyl group. Errors during amino acid recognition do not usually compromise the accuracy of translation due to highly specific aaRS enzymes, and the widespread existence of editing mechanisms that proofread non-cognate amino acids. For example, phenylalanine tRNA synthetase (PheRS) edits mischarged Tyr-tRNAPhe at a hydrolytic editing site ∼30 Å from the synthetic active site (Roy et al., 2004; Kotik-Kogan et al., 2005). PheRS editing provides a key checkpoint in quality control, as mischarged Tyr-tRNAPhe is readily delivered to the ribosome by EF-Tu where it can efficiently decode Phe codons as Tyr in the growing polypeptide chain, resulting in mistranslation (Ling et al., 2007b, 2009). Despite their role in accurately translating the genetic code, aaRS editing pathways are not conserved, and their activities have varying effects on cell viability (Bacher et al., 2005; Lee et al., 2006; Bacher and Schimmel, 2007; Bacher et al., 2007). Mycoplasma mobile, for example, tolerates relatively high error rates during translation and lacks PheRS editing function, as do other aaRSs in this organism (Li et al., 2011; Yadavalli and Ibba, 2013). Saccharomyces cerevisiae cytoplasmic PheRS (ScctPheRS) has a low Phe/Tyr specificity and is capable of editing, whereas the yeast mitochondrial enzyme (ScmtPheRS) completely lacks an editing domain, and instead relies on high Phe/Tyr specificity. Escherichia coli, in contrast, has retained both features and displays a high degree of Phe/Tyr specificity and robust editing activity (Reynolds et al., 2010). The range of divergent mechanisms used by different PheRSs to discriminate against non-cognate amino acids illustrates how the requirements for translation quality control vary with cellular physiology (Yadavalli and Ibba, 2013). Furthermore, given that editing by PheRS and other aaRSs is not essential for viability in yeast or E. coli, it is clear that the true roles of these quality control pathways remain to be fully elucidated (Reynolds et al., 2010). In addition to the well-documented ability of aaRSs to edit tRNAs charged with genetically encoded near cognate amino acids, these same proofreading activities have been demonstrated to act on other non-canonical substrates. AaRSs are able to edit tRNAs misacylated with a range of amino acids not found in the genetic code such as homocysteine, norleucine, α-aminobutyrate and meta-tyrosine (m-Tyr), although the physiological relevance of these activities is unknown (reviewed in Yadavalli and Ibba, 2012). Both E. coli and Thermus thermophilus PheRS have been shown to edit m-Tyr, a metabolic byproduct formed by oxidation of phenylalanine following metal-catalyzed formation of hydroxyl radical species (Huggins et al., 1993; Stadtman and Levine, 2003; Klipcan et al., 2009). Certain species of fescue grasses (Festuca spp.) produce m-Tyr as a natural defense agent that appears in the proteomes of neighboring plants, and m-Tyr accumulation in the proteome of Chinese hamster ovary (CHO) cells has been proposed to have a cytotoxic effect on translation (Gurer-Orhan et al., 2006; Bertin et al., 2007). Taken together, these findings suggest that oxidative stress could potentially result in m-Tyr accumulation with the accompanying threat of cytotoxic mistranslation. Under such growth conditions, the ability of the cell to edit m-Tyr-tRNAPhe would be essential to maintain cellular viability. Here we show that bacterial PheRS is able to efficiently edit m-Tyr-tRNAPhe, and that this editing activity is essential for cellular growth and survival under both cytotoxic amino acid and oxidative stress conditions. Additionally, we show that PheRS editing in yeast provides only limited protection from m-Tyr, but instead is essential for protecting the cell from para-Tyr-tRNAPhe accumulation. ## Results ### PheRS editing is dispensable for E. coli and S. cerevisiae growth To investigate the role of E. coli PheRS (EcPheRS) editing in vivo, a strain was constructed containing a point mutation (G318W) within pheT, which encodes the β subunit of PheRS. Changes to residue βG318 hinder access to the editing site and thereby reduce EcPheRS posttransfer editing activity by more than 70-fold in vitro (Roy et al., 2004; Ling et al., 2007a). E. coli strain NP37, which encodes a temperature sensitive pheS allele, was used as the background strain in order to facilitate selection of recombinant strains (Kast et al., 1992). Cell-free extracts from non-temperature-sensitive NP37-derived strains with wild type pheT and pheT(G318W) alleles were prepared and their PheRS activities tested. Only the strain encoding wild type PheRS retained post–transfer editing activity against p-Tyr-tRNAPhe (Figure 1A). Both strains showed identical levels of aminoacylation activity and growth at 37°C, indicating that the proofreading pathway is not required for growth under normal laboratory conditions. The role of PheRS editing was also investigated in S. cerevisiae by mutation of the chromosomal FRS1 gene, which encodes the β-subunit of cytoplasmic PheRS (ScctPheRS). Introduction in FRS1 of a mutation encoding the amino acid replacement D243A eliminated p-Tyr-tRNAPhe editing in vivo (Figure 1B; Reynolds et al., 2010) and had no effect on growth compared to wild type under standard conditions. ![Figure 1.](https://cdn.elifesciences.org/articles/02501/elife-02501-fig1-v2.jpg) **Figure 1.:** (A) Post–transfer hydrolysis of [14C]- Tyr-tRNAPhe (1 µM) by cell-free extracts isolated from wild type (●) and pheT(G318W) (■) E. coli strains (140 mg/ml total protein concentration) or buffer (▲) at 37°C. (B) Posttransfer editing activity of βD243A ctPheRS in S. cerevisiae. Reactions were performed at 37°C with 2 μM Tyr-tRNAPhe and S. cerevisiae wild type FRS1 or frs1-1 (D243A) cell-free extracts normalized to aminoacylation activity (Reynolds et al., 2010). Data points are the mean of at least three independent experiments, with errors bars representing ±1 SD. ### PheRS editing specifies m-Tyr resistance in E. coli Phenotypic microarrays (Biolog) were used to compare the growth of E. coli pheT(G318W) to wild type under 1920 growth conditions, and no significant changes were observed in the absence of PheRS editing. Additional experiments to investigate possible roles for editing under a range of other conditions, including heat shock, cold shock, pH stress and aging, failed to reveal differences compared to wild type. Growth of these strains was also compared in media containing varying concentrations of near-cognate p-Tyr in order to test the limits of EcPheRS specificity in the absence of post–transfer editing activity. Elevated concentrations of p-Tyr (>3 mM) did not affect the growth of E. coli pheT(G318W) compared to wild type (Figure 2A). Analysis of amino acid pools extracted from representative cells showed E. coli pheT(G318W) contained similar intracellular concentrations of p-Tyr and Phe as the wild type strain, indicating the pheT mutation has no effect on amino acid uptake (Table 1). In the absence of amino acid supplementation, the intracellular Phe:p-Tyr ratios were 1:1, and rose to 1:9 upon addition of p-Tyr. The growth of E. coli pheT(G318W) in the presence of m-Tyr, a non-proteinogenic amino acid previously shown to be a substrate for bacterial PheRS, was then investigated (Klipcan et al., 2009). Relative to wild type, growth of E. coli strain pheT(G318W) was inhibited in the presence of elevated intracellular concentrations of m-Tyr suggesting PheRS proofreading activity is needed to clear mischarged m-Tyr-tRNAPhe in vivo (Table 1; Figure 2B). Editing assays performed in vitro confirmed that, as with p-Tyr, post–transfer editing of m-Tyr-tRNAPhe by PheRS is ablated by the G318W mutation (Figure 2—figure supplement 1). The inhibitory effect of m-Tyr on growth in the absence of editing was also observed in E. coli mutants derived from strain MG1655 that, unlike the NP37 background, encodes an intact stringent response (Figure 2C). The pheT editing mutation was also constructed in the MG1655 background in order to confirm the m-Tyr growth phenotype was not specific to strains lacking the stringent response, where cells are unable to properly sense and respond to amino acid starvation. Growth of E. coli pheT(G318W) was also evaluated in the presence of ortho-tyrosine (o-Tyr) and 3,4-dihydroxy-L-phenylalanine (L-DOPA), oxidation products of Phe and p-Tyr, respectively (Maskos et al., 1992). At elevated p-Tyr concentrations, growth of the frs1-1 (D243A) strain was restricted compared to wild type (Figure 3A), while the growth of both strains was more comparably inhibited by addition of m-Tyr (Figure 3B). Data points are the mean of three independent cultures, with errors bars representing ±1 SD. ### Bacterial and eukaryotic PheRSs have divergent tyrosine isomer specificities E. coli PheRS is able to edit preformed m-Tyr-tRNAPhe (Klipcan et al., 2009), and the loss of this activity in the G318W variant indicates that editing occurs at the site previously described for p-Tyr-tRNAPhe (Ling et al., 2007a; Figure 2—figure supplement 1). Wild type EcPheRS did not stably charge tRNAPhe with either m- or p-Tyr, while G318W utilized both isomers for aminoacylation, with m-tyr being a more efficient substrate (Figure 4A,B). Under similar conditions, G318W PheRS was unable to utilize o-Tyr or L-DOPA for tRNAPhe aminoacylation, consistent with the absence of any growth phenotype of the pheT(G318W) strain in the presence of these tyrosine analogs (Figure 2—figure supplement 2). As a substrate for T. thermophilus PheRS, L-DOPA has been shown to be 1500-fold less efficient than Phe (Moor et al., 2011). Examination of amino acid substrate specificity showed the catalytic efficiency (kcat/KM) for m-Tyr activation by EcPheRS to be 35-fold less than for Phe, in contrast to p-Tyr which is activated almost 3000-fold less efficiently than the cognate substrate (Table 2). The ability of EcPheRS to efficiently activate m-Tyr is consistent with the need for editing to maintain cellular viability during growth in the presence of this non-proteinogenic amino acid. ![Figure 4.](https://cdn.elifesciences.org/articles/02501/elife-02501-fig4-v2.jpg) **Figure 4.:** tRNAPhe aminoacylation activities of (A) wild type and (B) G318W E. coli PheRS for 60 μM cognate Phe and non-cognate p- and m-Tyr substrates. In contrast to the E. coli enzyme, wild type ScctPheRS efficiently utilizes m-Tyr for activation and aminoacylation of tRNAPhe. Charging of tRNAPhe with m-Tyr was seen at amino acid substrate concentrations where p-Tyr-tRNAPhe synthesis was not detected (Figure 4C; Table 2). The kcat/KM of m-Tyr activation by ScctPheRS is 71-fold lower than that of Phe, demonstrating relatively poor discrimination between the two amino acids (Table 2). In contrast to the E. coli enzyme, p-Tyr-tRNAPhe is a better substrate for post–transfer editing by ScctPheRS relative to m-Tyr-tRNAPhe (Figure 5). These results provide a possible explanation for the toxic effects m-Tyr has on the wild type yeast strain (Figure 3B), although additional cytotoxic affects of m-Tyr outside of translation cannot be ruled out. Post–transfer editing of m-Tyr-tRNAPhe by ScctPheRS provides some protection from m-Tyr’s toxic affects as there is a difference in the growth of wild type vs the frs1-1(D243A) strain at high concentrations of m-Tyr (Figure 3B). The mitochondrial variant of yeast PheRS (ScmtPheRS), which naturally lacks Tyr-tRNAPhe post–transfer editing activity (Roy et al., 2005), was also found to synthesize m-Tyr-tRNAPhe more efficiently than p-Tyr-tRNAPhe at similar tyrosine isomer concentrations (Figure 4D). The absence in yeast of appropriate quality control pathways in either the cytoplasm or mitochondria suggests that m-Tyr toxicity results from the accumulation of mischarged tRNAs in both compartments. ![Figure 5.](https://cdn.elifesciences.org/articles/02501/elife-02501-fig5-v2.jpg) **Figure 5.:** Hydrolysis of 0.1 µM yeast (A) p-Tyr-[32P]-tRNAPhe or (B) m-Tyr-[32P]-tRNAPhe in the presence of 10 nM wild type ScctPheRS (●) D243A ScctPheRS (■) or buffer (▲) at 37°C. Dipeptide synthesis was monitored in vitro using m-Tyr-tRNAPhe:EF-Tu:GTP as a substrate for decoding of a ribosomal A site Phe (UUC) codon. Under these conditions similar levels of fMet-m-Tyr and fMet-Phe were synthesized, indicating a lack of discrimination against the non-proteinogenic amino acid at the A-site of E. coli ribosomes (Figure 6A). ![Figure 6.](https://cdn.elifesciences.org/articles/02501/elife-02501-fig6-v2.jpg) **Figure 6.:** (A) In vitro 70S ribosomal di-peptide synthesis with either Phe-tRNAPhe or m-Tyr-tRNAPhe (B) LC-MS/MS-MRM quantification of m-Tyr and Phe in protein hydrolysis isolated from E. coli expressed as molar ratio of m-Tyr to Phe. Wild type and pheT(G318W) strains grown in in M9 minimal media alone and supplemented with p-Tyr are shown. Error bars represent ± standard error of means. ![Figure 6—figure supplement 2.](https://cdn.elifesciences.org/articles/02501/elife-02501-fig6-figsupp2-v2.jpg) **Figure 6—figure supplement 2.:** Aminoacylation of E. coli [32P]-tRNAPhe transcript (0.5 μM) with m-Tyr (1 mM) by E. coli TyrRS (50 nM) at 25°C. The effect of m-Tyr on protein synthesis in vivo was investigated by analyzing the accumulation of the non-proteinogenic amino acid in the proteomes of wild type and E. coli pheT(G318W) cells. Cytosolic protein samples were isolated from m-Tyr treated E. coli cells and samples subjected to acid hydrolysis to generate individual amino acids. The resulting amino acid hydrolysate was analyzed by liquid chromatography tandem mass spectrometry with multiple reaction monitoring (LC-MS/MS-MRM). To validate peak assignments of the Tyr isomers, co-chromatography was performed with synthetic m-Tyr or o-Tyr added to proteome samples. Only one peak for each of the isomers was observed, validating the assignments. Some level of m-Tyr was found to be present in the proteomes of both wild type and phe(G318W) strains indicating incorporation could be occurring through more than one route. Comparison of proteome total amino acid levels between wild type and pheT(G318W) strains indicated a level of misincorporation of 1% m-Tyr at Phe codons due to the absence of PheRS editing (Figure 6B). In wild type proteins the fraction of m-Tyr compared to Phe is 0.015, increasing to 0.025 in samples isolated from the pheT(G318W) strain grown in the same conditions. This result indicates post–transfer editing by PheRS provides protection of the E. coli proteome from misincorporation of m-Tyr at Phe codons. Quantification of p-Tyr relative to Phe in the protein samples isolated from cultures grown in the presence of 0.5 mM p-Tyr does not change between the wild type and pheT(G318W) strains indicating this protein amino acid is not significantly misincorporated at Phe codons, even in the absence of PheRS editing (Figure 6—figure supplement 1). These analyses show a ratio of p-Tyr/Phe of 0.6, which correlates reasonably well with previous estimates of amino acid usage in E. coli (0.7, Jauregui et al., 2000). A detectable level of m-Tyr in the proteome of wild type E. coli suggests either this non-proteinogenic amino acid escapes PheRS editing, infiltrates the proteome by means other than misincorporation at Phe codons or is carried over during cytosolic protein preparation. To measure the approximate amount of carryover, wild type PheRS E. coli strain was grown in the presence of 0.5 mM o-Tyr, which is not a substrate for protein synthesis, and total protein samples were subjected to acid hydrolysis and LC-MS/MS-MRM. In these samples, traces of o-Tyr were detected, indicating that free amino acid carry over possibly contributes to some of the m-Tyr detected in the samples from the wild type strain grown in M9 minimal media supplemented with m-Tyr. Whether the m-Tyr seen in the proteome of E. coli containing PheRS editing is formed post-translationally or is incorporated during protein synthesis via another promiscuous tRNA synthetase in E. coli is unclear. Aminoacylation of tRNATyr with m-Tyr by E. coli TyrRS was detected in vitro, suggesting this synthetase may provide a route of m-Tyr incorporation even when PheRS editing is active (Figure 6—figure supplement 2). ### E. coli PheRS editing is required for growth under oxidative stress conditions Reactive oxygen species (ROS) generated under oxidative stress via the Fenton reaction are capable of catalyzing the conversion of Phe to m-Tyr, which could potentially threaten the fidelity of protein synthesis in the absence of editing (Maskos et al., 1992; Stadtman and Levine, 2003). To investigate if oxidative stress conditions generate potentially toxic levels of m-Tyr in vivo, wild type and editing deficient E. coli were grown in the presence of H2O2 and FeSO4 (Fe2+) as a source of ROS. LC-MS/MS-MRM analyses showed that m-Tyr accumulated in the intracellular amino acid pools of ROS-treated cells (Figure 7A). In addition to m-Tyr, significant de novo o-Tyr accumulation was also observed following ROS treatment, although this is not expected to pose a threat to translation fidelity as it is not a substrate for PheRS (Figure 2—figure supplement 2). E. coli lacking PheRS editing activity showed a reduction in growth relative to wild type when grown in media where ROS exposure increased, consistent with the accumulation of free m-Tyr and its subsequent utilization in protein synthesis (Figure 7B). Taken together, our data indicate that PheRS editing activity affords E. coli protection against the co-translational insertion of non-proteinogenic amino acids that accumulate during oxidative stress. Attempts to identify m-Tyr in the total protein hydrolysis samples under oxidative stress conditions revealed the presence of m-Tyr and o-Tyr in both the wild type and pheT(G318W) strains. Proper quantification of the levels of each amino acid in these samples was not possible as adequate resolution could not be achieved for the peaks corresponding to the different Tyr isomers in total protein samples prepared from H2O2 treated cells. These observations suggest posttranslational damage of Phe residues in protein by H2O2 treatment may also be partially responsible for the accumulation of hydroxylated Phe residues. In efforts to increase the misincorporation of m-Tyr into the proteome at Phe codons, higher levels of H2O2 were used, however this resulted in the death of both strains likely due to the other damaging effects of reactive oxygen species. ![Figure 7.](https://cdn.elifesciences.org/articles/02501/elife-02501-fig7-v2.jpg) **Figure 7.:** (A) LC-MS/MS-MRM chromatograms for p-, m- and o-Tyr (m/z 182→136 transition) extracted from cells grown in the absence (left) and presence (right) of H2O2 and FeSO4. (B) Growth of E. coli pheT(G318W) strain relative to wild type in M9 minimal media supplemented with 0.1 mM FeSO4 and increasing concentrations of H2O2. Bars are the mean of three independent cultures, with errors bars representing ± SD. ## Discussion ### Context dependent specificity and editing It has long been proposed that the fidelity of aminoacyl-tRNA synthetases needs to be at or above 1 in 3,000, which is cited as an approximate overall level of error for protein synthesis (Loftfield and Vanderjagt, 1972). AaRS fidelity is achieved through discrimination at the aminoacylation site as well as through additional editing activities in some aaRSs. Protection against both p-Tyr and m-Tyr incorporation at Phe codons appears critical in E. coli as the PheRS enzyme maintains high active-site selectivity against p-Tyr as well as post–transfer editing activity against m-Tyr-tRNAPhe. E. coli PheRS requires this editing activity to protect the proteome from toxic effects of the non-proteinogenic amino acid m-Tyr, which is poorly discriminated against by the active site of the enzyme. Examination of the structure of the catalytic active site provides clues as to why PheRS is unable to discriminate against all the Tyr isomers. Ala294 is primarily responsible for specificity against binding of para-substituted Phe analogs, while Gln174 and Glu210 help stabilize the hydroxyl of non-cognate m-Tyr at position 3 of the ring (E. coli numbering) (Klipcan et al., 2009). In the case of the cognate Phe substrate, Glu210 is also needed to hydrogen bond with the Phe amino group, ensuring correct orientation of the substrate for activation (Safro et al., 2005; Mermershtain et al., 2011). It is unlikely this enzyme selects against recognition of m-Tyr while still maintaining efficient activity for the cognate amino acid, therefore the maintenance of post–transfer editing activity is critical for fidelity in E. coli. In eukaryotes, cytoplasmic PheRS editing is needed to protect the proteome from p-Tyr misincorporation. This finding concurs with the low Phe/p-Tyr specificity of the yeast cytoplasmic enzyme (Reynolds et al., 2010). It is unclear if protection from m-Tyr incorporation is achieved through editing as the yeast strain encoding wild type ctPheRS is sensitive to high concentrations of m-Tyr, mtPheRS efficiently aminoacylates m-Tyr onto tRNAPhe, and other eukaryotic proteomes are vulnerable to the use of this oxygen-damaged amino acid for translation (Gurer-Orhan et al., 2006). Taken together, these findings suggest that either m-Tyr accumulation is not a substantial threat in eukaryotes, or possibly that the incorporation of low amounts of this non-proteinogenic amino acid in certain proteomes confers some as yet unknown evolutionary benefits. ### Non-proteinogenic amino acids as threats to translational integrity Naturally occurring non-proteinogenic amino acids occur widely in nature and are well-characterized by-products and/or intermediates of biosynthetic pathways (Richmond, 1962). The actual threats these non-canonical substrates pose to protein synthesis and cell viability is unknown, as is the role of aaRS quality control in protecting the proteome from such amino acids. The non-proteinogenic amino acid m-Tyr has been detected in several eukaryotic proteomes and is one of the products of canonical aromatic amino acid oxidation (Wells-Knecht et al., 1993; Pennathur et al., 2001). The presence of hydroxylated forms of tyrosine in proteomes has previously been attributed to post-translational damage to proteins by hydroxyl radical species, and is often used as a marker for tissue damage due to the oxidative conditions of aging and disease. It has also been shown that m-Tyr and other Tyr analogs, for example L-DOPA, are substrates for translation in some organisms and could potentially be incorporated directly during protein synthesis (Rodgers et al., 2002; Ozawa et al., 2005; Gurer-Orhan et al., 2006; Klipcan et al., 2009; Moor et al., 2011). Our results now reveal the role of E. coli PheRS editing for preventing the use of m-Tyr during protein synthesis, demonstrating the threat amino acid oxidation poses to the proper functioning of the bacterial translation machinery. Incorporation of m-Tyr into the proteome of E. coli at Phe codons is toxic to the cell, and in the absence of PheRS quality control this non-proteinogenic amino acid serves as an efficient substrate for translation. Other non-proteinogenic amino acids have also been shown to be potential threats to translation, such as α-aminobutyrate, which in the absence of ValRS editing is toxic at high concentrations, although the physiological conditions under which this non-protein amino acid might naturally accumulate to significant levels are unclear (Nangle et al., 2002). The robust editing activity maintained by E. coli PheRS to protect the proteome from m-Tyr demonstrates the significant threat such an amino acid poses when misincorporated at specific near-cognate codons. In contrast, the presence of m-Tyr in the proteome of wild type E. coli suggests misincorporation can also occur at Tyr codons but without cytotoxic sequelae. These findings suggest that the cellular effects of non-proteinogenic amino acid incorporation are codon-dependent. The cell does not have codons or tRNAs for m-Tyr, therefore any advantage or disadvantage this amino acid might provide to the proteome cannot easily be selected for, or against, at the level of the genetic code. The only selection against near-cognate non-proteinogenic amino acid use during translation can be made at the level of the synthetase or ternary complex formation with an elongation factor (Dale and Uhlenbeck, 2005). In E. coli, misincorporation of m-Tyr at Phe codons in the absence of PheRS quality control occurred at a frequency of 1% and had a significant impact on cellular viability and restricted growth. This contrasts with the effects of misincorporation of canonical amino acids, which have been shown to be tolerated at rates of up to 10% without inhibiting growth (Ruan et al., 2008). Taken together with earlier studies, our present findings now show that the misincorporation of non-proteinogenic amino acids presents a substantial challenge for protein synthesis quality control. This in turn suggests that many ‘dispensable’ editing functions, both in aaRSs and trans editing factors, may actually be essential for growth under conditions that lead to the accumulation of potentially toxic levels of non-proteinogenic amino acids. ### Oxidative stress and translation quality control Oxidation of amino acids by reactive species such as hydroxyl radical and superoxide anions results in limited alteration of amino acid structure, such as the addition of a hydroxyl group, creating potential in vivo substrates for tRNA misacylation. These damaged amino acids challenge the protein synthesis machinery, as for example in the case of L-DOPA, and leucine hydroxide, which have been shown to be incorporated into proteins in mouse cells (Rodgers et al., 2002; Ozawa et al., 2005). The formation of intracellular m-Tyr in E. coli under physiological conditions is possibly a result of cellular exposure to H2O2. Aerobic respiration results in elevated endogenous levels of H2O2, but bacterial cells are also exposed to ROS present in their environment. Uncharged H2O2 is able to penetrate the cell membrane and accumulate inside cells whenever H2O2 is present in the extracellular habitat. At physiological pH, H2O2 quickly oxidizes ferrous iron via the Fenton reaction, generating a hydroxyl radical that can react with nearby cellular targets (Rush et al., 1990). Accumulation of toxic levels of m-Tyr in the intracellular pools of E. coli occurs under experimental conditions that promote the formation of hydroxyl radicals, however this is not the major byproduct of Phe oxidation. The o-Tyr isomer is the more abundant hydroxylation product under ROS-generating conditions used here (Figure 7). However, there is no observed o-Tyr aminoacylation of tRNAPhe by wild type PheRS in vitro, or inhibition of cell growth, in the presence of this hydroxylated Phe substrate. These, and the corresponding biochemical data, indicate how E. coli PheRS has evolved to effectively discriminate against different Tyr isomers using a combination of substrate specificity (o-Tyr, p-Tyr) and editing activity (m-Tyr, p-Tyr). In contrast, yeast PheRS has mainly evolved specifically to discriminate for p-Tyr by editing, reflecting differences in the factors that drive selection of quality control mechanisms. ## Materials and methods ### Strains, plasmids, and general methods Proteins and tRNAs were prepared essentially as described previously (Roy et al., 2005). claims.source: Both E. coli and Thermus thermophilus PheRS have been shown to edit m-Tyr, a metabolic byproduct formed by oxidation of phenylalanine following metal-catalyzed formation of hydroxyl radical species (Huggins et al., 1993; Stadtman and Levine, 2003; Klipcan et al., 2009).
claims.evidence: This is supported by citations to studies on oxidative damage.

claims.claim: Certain species of fescue grasses (Festuca spp.) produce m-Tyr as a natural defense agent that appears in the proteomes of neighboring plants.
claims.source: Certain species of fescue grasses (Festuca spp.) produce m-Tyr as a natural defense agent that appears in the proteomes of neighboring plants, and m-Tyr accumulation in the proteome of Chinese hamster ovary (CHO) cells has been proposed to have a cytotoxic effect on translation (Gurer-Orhan et al., 2006; Bertin et al., 2007).
claims.evidence: This is supported by citations to studies on fescue grasses.

claims.claim: m-Tyr accumulation in the proteome of Chinese hamster ovary (CHO) cells has been proposed to have a cytotoxic effect on translation.
claims.source: Certain species of fescue grasses (Festuca spp.) produce m-Tyr as a natural defense agent that appears in the proteomes of neighboring plants, and m-Tyr accumulation in the proteome of Chinese hamster ovary (CHO) cells has been proposed to have a cytotoxic effect on translation (Gurer-Orhan et al., 2006; Bertin et al., 2007).
claims.evidence: This is supported by citations to studies on CHO cells.

claims.claim: Bacterial PheRS is able to efficiently edit m-Tyr-tRNAPhe.
claims.source: Here we show that bacterial PheRS is able to efficiently edit m-Tyr-tRNAPhe, and that this editing activity is essential for cellular growth and survival under both cytotoxic amino acid and oxidative stress conditions.
claims.evidence: This is demonstrated by in vitro editing assays shown in the manuscript.

claims.claim: PheRS editing activity is essential for cellular growth and survival under both cytotoxic amino acid and oxidative stress conditions.
claims.source: Here we show that bacterial PheRS is able to efficiently edit m-Tyr-tRNAPhe, and that this editing activity is essential for cellular growth and survival under both cytotoxic amino acid and oxidative stress conditions.
claims.evidence: This is demonstrated by growth assays under m-Tyr and oxidative stress conditions.

claims.claim: PheRS editing in yeast provides only limited protection from m-Tyr.
claims.source: Additionally, we show that PheRS editing in yeast provides only limited protection from m-Tyr, but instead is essential for protecting the cell from para-Tyr-tRNAPhe accumulation.
claims.evidence: This is demonstrated by yeast growth assays showing sensitivity to m-Tyr even in wild-type strains.

claims.claim: PheRS editing in yeast is essential for protecting the cell from para-Tyr-tRNAPhe accumulation.
claims.source: Additionally, we show that PheRS editing in yeast provides only limited protection from m-Tyr, but instead is essential for protecting the cell from para-Tyr-tRNAPhe accumulation.
claims.evidence: This is demonstrated by yeast growth assays showing editing-deficient strains are sensitive to p-Tyr.

claims.claim: The G318W mutation in E. coli PheRS reduces posttransfer editing activity by more than 70-fold in vitro.
claims.source: Changes to residue βG318 hinder access to the editing site and thereby reduce EcPheRS posttransfer editing activity by more than 70-fold in vitro (Roy et al., 2004; Ling et al., 2007a).
claims.evidence: This is supported by citations to previous biochemical studies.

claims.claim: Only the E. coli strain encoding wild type PheRS retained post-transfer editing activity against p-Tyr-tRNAPhe.
claims.source: Only the strain encoding wild type PheRS retained post–transfer editing activity against p-Tyr-tRNAPhe (Figure 1A).
claims.evidence: This is demonstrated by the editing assay shown in Figure 1A.

claims.claim: E. coli strains with wild type pheT and pheT(G318W) alleles showed identical levels of aminoacylation activity and growth at 37°C.
claims.source: Both strains showed identical levels of aminoacylation activity and growth at 37°C, indicating that the proofreading pathway is not required for growth under normal laboratory conditions.
claims.evidence: This is based on experimental observations of growth and enzyme activity.

claims.claim: The proofreading pathway is not required for E. coli growth under normal laboratory conditions.
claims.source: Both strains showed identical levels of aminoacylation activity and growth at 37°C, indicating that the proofreading pathway is not required for growth under normal laboratory conditions.
claims.evidence: This is inferred from the observation that editing-deficient strains grow normally under standard conditions.

claims.claim: The D243A mutation in S. cerevisiae FRS1 eliminated p-Tyr-tRNAPhe editing in vivo.
claims.source: Introduction in FRS1 of a mutation encoding the amino acid replacement D243A eliminated p-Tyr-tRNAPhe editing in vivo (Figure 1B; Reynolds et al., 2010) and had no effect on growth compared to wild type under standard conditions.
claims.evidence: This is demonstrated by the editing assay shown in Figure 1B and cited work.

claims.claim: The D243A mutation in S. cerevisiae FRS1 had no effect on growth compared to wild type under standard conditions.
claims.source: Introduction in FRS1 of a mutation encoding the amino acid replacement D243A eliminated p-Tyr-tRNAPhe editing in vivo (Figure 1B; Reynolds et al., 2010) and had no effect on growth compared to wild type under standard conditions.
claims.evidence: This is based on experimental growth observations.

claims.claim: Phenotypic microarrays revealed no significant changes in growth of E. coli pheT(G318W) compared to wild type under 1920 growth conditions.
claims.source: Phenotypic microarrays (Biolog) were used to compare the growth of E. coli pheT(G318W) to wild type under 1920 growth conditions, and no significant changes were observed in the absence of PheRS editing.
claims.evidence: This is based on experimental phenotypic microarray data.

claims.claim: Elevated concentrations of p-Tyr (>3 mM) did not affect the growth of E. coli pheT(G318W) compared to wild type.
claims.source: Elevated concentrations of p-Tyr (>3 mM) did not affect the growth of E. coli pheT(G318W) compared to wild type (Figure 2A).
claims.evidence: This is demonstrated by the growth assay shown in Figure 2A.

claims.claim: E. coli pheT(G318W) contained similar intracellular concentrations of p-Tyr and Phe as the wild type strain.
claims.source: Analysis of amino acid pools extracted from representative cells showed E. coli pheT(G318W) contained similar intracellular concentrations of p-Tyr and Phe as the wild type strain, indicating the pheT mutation has no effect on amino acid uptake (Table 1).
claims.evidence: This is demonstrated by amino acid pool measurements shown in Table 1.

claims.claim: The pheT mutation has no effect on amino acid uptake in E. coli.
claims.source: Analysis of amino acid pools extracted from representative cells showed E. coli pheT(G318W) contained similar intracellular concentrations of p-Tyr and Phe as the wild type strain, indicating the pheT mutation has no effect on amino acid uptake (Table 1).
claims.evidence: This is inferred from the observation that intracellular amino acid concentrations are similar between strains.

claims.claim: Growth of E. coli strain pheT(G318W) was inhibited in the presence of elevated intracellular concentrations of m-Tyr.
claims.source: Relative to wild type, growth of E. coli strain pheT(G318W) was inhibited in the presence of elevated intracellular concentrations of m-Tyr suggesting PheRS proofreading activity is needed to clear mischarged m-Tyr-tRNAPhe in vivo (Table 1; Figure 2B).
claims.evidence: This is demonstrated by growth assays shown in Figure 2B and Table 1.

claims.claim: PheRS proofreading activity is needed to clear mischarged m-Tyr-tRNAPhe in vivo.
claims.source: Relative to wild type, growth of E. coli strain pheT(G318W) was inhibited in the presence of elevated intracellular concentrations of m-Tyr suggesting PheRS proofreading activity is needed to clear mischarged m-Tyr-tRNAPhe in vivo (Table 1; Figure 2B).
claims.evidence: This is inferred from the growth inhibition of editing-deficient strains in the presence of m-Tyr.

claims.claim: Post-transfer editing of m-Tyr-tRNAPhe by PheRS is ablated by the G318W mutation.
claims.source: Editing assays performed in vitro confirmed that, as with p-Tyr, post–transfer editing of m-Tyr-tRNAPhe by PheRS is ablated by the G318W mutation (Figure 2—figure supplement 1).
claims.evidence: This is demonstrated by in vitro editing assays shown in Figure 2—figure supplement 1.

claims.claim: The inhibitory effect of m-Tyr on growth in the absence of editing was also observed in E. coli mutants derived from strain MG1655.
claims.source: The inhibitory effect of m-Tyr on growth in the absence of editing was also observed in E. coli mutants derived from strain MG1655 that, unlike the NP37 background, encodes an intact stringent response (Figure 2C).
claims.evidence: This is demonstrated by growth assays in the MG1655 background shown in Figure 2C.

claims.claim: Neither o-Tyr nor L-DOPA inhibited growth of wild type or the pheT(G318W) mutant E. coli strain.
claims.source: Growth of E. coli pheT(G318W) was also evaluated in the presence of ortho-tyrosine (o-Tyr) and 3,4-dihydroxy-L-phenylalanine (L-DOPA), oxidation products of Phe and p-Tyr, respectively (Maskos et al., 1992). Neither of these non-proteinogenic amino acids inhibited growth of wild type or the pheT(G318W) mutant E. coli strain (Figure 2—figure supplement 2).
claims.evidence: This is demonstrated by growth assays shown in Figure 2—figure supplement 2.

claims.claim: The editing deficient frs1-1 (D243A) yeast strain showed a pronounced defect in p-Tyr resistance.
claims.source: While the editing deficient frs1-1 (D243A) yeast strain displayed no difference to wild type under heat shock or ethanol stress, it showed a pronounced defect in p-Tyr resistance. At elevated p-Tyr concentrations, growth of the frs1-1 (D243A) strain was restricted compared to wild type (Figure 3A)
claims.evidence: This is demonstrated by growth assays shown in Figure 3A.

claims.claim: The growth of both wild type and frs1-1 (D243A) yeast strains was comparably inhibited by addition of m-Tyr.
claims.source: while the growth of both strains was more comparably inhibited by addition of m-Tyr (Figure 3B).
claims.evidence: This is demonstrated by growth assays shown in Figure 3B.

claims.claim: Wild type EcPheRS did not stably charge tRNAPhe with either m- or p-Tyr.
claims.source: Wild type EcPheRS did not stably charge tRNAPhe with either m- or p-Tyr, while G318W utilized both isomers for aminoacylation, with m-tyr being a more efficient substrate (Figure 4A,B).
claims.evidence: This is demonstrated by aminoacylation assays shown in Figure 4A,B.

claims.claim: G318W EcPheRS utilized both m-Tyr and p-Tyr for aminoacylation, with m-Tyr being a more efficient substrate.
claims.source: Wild type EcPheRS did not stably charge tRNAPhe with either m- or p-Tyr, while G318W utilized both isomers for aminoacylation, with m-tyr being a more efficient substrate (Figure 4A,B).
claims.evidence: This is demonstrated by aminoacylation assays shown in Figure 4A,B.

claims.claim: G318W PheRS was unable to utilize o-Tyr or L-DOPA for tRNAPhe aminoacylation.
claims.source: Under similar conditions, G318W PheRS was unable to utilize o-Tyr or L-DOPA for tRNAPhe aminoacylation, consistent with the absence of any growth phenotype of the pheT(G318W) strain in the presence of these tyrosine analogs (Figure 2—figure supplement 2).
claims.evidence: This is demonstrated by aminoacylation assays shown in Figure 2—figure supplement 2.

claims.claim: The catalytic efficiency (kcat/KM) for m-Tyr activation by EcPheRS is 35-fold less than for Phe.
claims.source: Examination of amino acid substrate specificity showed the catalytic efficiency (kcat/KM) for m-Tyr activation by EcPheRS to be 35-fold less than for Phe, in contrast to p-Tyr which is activated almost 3000-fold less efficiently than the cognate substrate (Table 2).
claims.evidence: This is demonstrated by kinetic data shown in Table 2.

claims.claim: p-Tyr is activated almost 3000-fold less efficiently than Phe by EcPheRS.
claims.source: Examination of amino acid substrate specificity showed the catalytic efficiency (kcat/KM) for m-Tyr activation by EcPheRS to be 35-fold less than for Phe, in contrast to p-Tyr which is activated almost 3000-fold less efficiently than the cognate substrate (Table 2).
claims.evidence: This is demonstrated by kinetic data shown in Table 2.

claims.claim: Wild type ScctPheRS efficiently utilizes m-Tyr for activation and aminoacylation of tRNAPhe.
claims.source: In contrast to the E. coli enzyme, wild type ScctPheRS efficiently utilizes m-Tyr for activation and aminoacylation of tRNAPhe. Charging of tRNAPhe with m-Tyr was seen at amino acid substrate concentrations where p-Tyr-tRNAPhe synthesis was not detected (Figure 4C; Table 2).
claims.evidence: This is demonstrated by aminoacylation assays shown in Figure 4C and kinetic data in Table 2.

claims.claim: The kcat/KM of m-Tyr activation by ScctPheRS is 71-fold lower than that of Phe.
claims.source: The kcat/KM of m-Tyr activation by ScctPheRS is 71-fold lower than that of Phe, demonstrating relatively poor discrimination between the two amino acids (Table 2).
claims.evidence: This is demonstrated by kinetic data shown in Table 2.

claims.claim: p-Tyr-tRNAPhe is a better substrate for post-transfer editing by ScctPheRS relative to m-Tyr-tRNAPhe.
claims.source: In contrast to the E. coli enzyme, p-Tyr-tRNAPhe is a better substrate for post–transfer editing by ScctPheRS relative to m-Tyr-tRNAPhe (Figure 5).
claims.evidence: This is demonstrated by editing assays shown in Figure 5.

claims.claim: The mitochondrial variant of yeast PheRS (ScmtPheRS) synthesizes m-Tyr-tRNAPhe more efficiently than p-Tyr-tRNAPhe at similar tyrosine isomer concentrations.
claims.source: The mitochondrial variant of yeast PheRS (ScmtPheRS), which naturally lacks Tyr-tRNAPhe post–transfer editing activity (Roy et al., 2005), was also found to synthesize m-Tyr-tRNAPhe more efficiently than p-Tyr-tRNAPhe at similar tyrosine isomer concentrations (Figure 4D).
claims.evidence: This is demonstrated by aminoacylation assays shown in Figure 4D.

claims.claim: Similar levels of fMet-m-Tyr and fMet-Phe were synthesized in vitro using m-Tyr-tRNAPhe:EF-Tu:GTP as a substrate for decoding of a ribosomal A site Phe (UUC) codon.
claims.source: Dipeptide synthesis was monitored in vitro using m-Tyr-tRNAPhe:EF-Tu:GTP as a substrate for decoding of a ribosomal A site Phe (UUC) codon. Under these conditions similar levels of fMet-m-Tyr and fMet-Phe were synthesized, indicating a lack of discrimination against the non-proteinogenic amino acid at the A-site of E. coli ribosomes (Figure 6A).
claims.evidence: This is demonstrated by dipeptide synthesis assays shown in Figure 6A.

claims.claim: There is a lack of discrimination against m-Tyr at the A-site of E. coli ribosomes.
claims.source: Under these conditions similar levels of fMet-m-Tyr and fMet-Phe were synthesized, indicating a lack of discrimination against the non-proteinogenic amino acid at the A-site of E. coli ribosomes (Figure 6A).
claims.evidence: This is inferred from the observation that similar levels of dipeptides are formed with m-Tyr and Phe.

claims.claim: Comparison of proteome total amino acid levels between wild type and pheT(G318W) strains indicated a level of misincorporation of 1% m-Tyr at Phe codons due to the absence of PheRS editing.
claims.source: Comparison of proteome total amino acid levels between wild type and pheT(G318W) strains indicated a level of misincorporation of 1% m-Tyr at Phe codons due to the absence of PheRS editing (Figure 6B).
claims.evidence: This is demonstrated by LC-MS/MS-MRM analysis shown in Figure 6B.

claims.claim: In wild type E. coli proteins the fraction of m-Tyr compared to Phe is 0.015, increasing to 0.025 in samples isolated from the pheT(G318W) strain grown in the same conditions.
claims.source: In wild type proteins the fraction of m-Tyr compared to Phe is 0.015, increasing to 0.025 in samples isolated from the pheT(G318W) strain grown in the same conditions.
claims.evidence: This is based on LC-MS/MS-MRM quantification of amino acids in protein hydrolysates.

claims.claim: Post-transfer editing by PheRS provides protection of the E. coli proteome from misincorporation of m-Tyr at Phe codons.
claims.source: This result indicates post–transfer editing by PheRS provides protection of the E. coli proteome from misincorporation of m-Tyr at Phe codons.
claims.evidence: This is inferred from the increased m-Tyr/Phe ratio in editing-deficient strains.

claims.claim: Quantification of p-Tyr relative to Phe in protein samples does not change between the wild type and pheT(G318W) strains.
claims.source: Quantification of p-Tyr relative to Phe in the protein samples isolated from cultures grown in the presence of 0.5 mM p-Tyr does not change between the wild type and pheT(G318W) strains indicating this protein amino acid is not significantly misincorporated at Phe codons, even in the absence of PheRS editing (Figure 6—figure supplement 1).
claims.evidence: This is demonstrated by LC-MS/MS-MRM analysis shown in Figure 6—figure supplement 1.

claims.claim: p-Tyr is not significantly misincorporated at Phe codons, even in the absence of PheRS editing.
claims.source: Quantification of p-Tyr relative to Phe in the protein samples isolated from cultures grown in the presence of 0.5 mM p-Tyr does not change between the wild type and pheT(G318W) strains indicating this protein amino acid is not significantly misincorporated at Phe codons, even in the absence of PheRS editing (Figure 6—figure supplement 1).
claims.evidence: This is inferred from the lack of change in p-Tyr/Phe ratio between strains.

claims.claim: Aminoacylation of tRNATyr with m-Tyr by E. coli TyrRS was detected in vitro.
claims.source: Aminoacylation of tRNATyr with m-Tyr by E. coli TyrRS was detected in vitro, suggesting this synthetase may provide a route of m-Tyr incorporation even when PheRS editing is active (Figure 6—figure supplement 2).
claims.evidence: This is demonstrated by aminoacylation assays shown in Figure 6—figure supplement 2.

claims.claim: E. coli TyrRS may provide a route of m-Tyr incorporation even when PheRS editing is active.
claims.source: Aminoacylation of tRNATyr with m-Tyr by E. coli TyrRS was detected in vitro, suggesting this synthetase may provide a route of m-Tyr incorporation even when PheRS editing is active (Figure 6—figure supplement 2).
claims.evidence: This is speculated based on the observation that TyrRS can charge tRNATyr with m-Tyr.

claims.claim: Reactive oxygen species (ROS) generated under oxidative stress via the Fenton reaction are capable of catalyzing the conversion of Phe to m-Tyr.
claims.source: Reactive oxygen species (ROS) generated under oxidative stress via the Fenton reaction are capable of catalyzing the conversion of Phe to m-Tyr, which could potentially threaten the fidelity of protein synthesis in the absence of editing (Maskos et al., 1992; Stadtman and Levine, 2003).
claims.evidence: This is supported by citations to studies on oxidative damage.

claims.claim: m-Tyr accumulated in the intracellular amino acid pools of ROS-treated E. coli cells.
claims.source: LC-MS/MS-MRM analyses showed that m-Tyr accumulated in the intracellular amino acid pools of ROS-treated cells (Figure 7A).
claims.evidence: This is demonstrated by LC-MS/MS-MRM analysis shown in Figure 7A.

claims.claim: Significant de novo o-Tyr accumulation was observed following ROS treatment of E. coli cells.
claims.source: In addition to m-Tyr, significant de novo o-Tyr accumulation was also observed following ROS treatment, although this is not expected to pose a threat to translation fidelity as it is not a substrate for PheRS (Figure 2—figure supplement 2).
claims.evidence: This is demonstrated by LC-MS/MS-MRM analysis shown in Figure 7A.

claims.claim: o-Tyr is not expected to pose a threat to translation fidelity as it is not a substrate for PheRS.
claims.source: In addition to m-Tyr, significant de novo o-Tyr accumulation was also observed following ROS treatment, although this is not expected to pose a threat to translation fidelity as it is not a substrate for PheRS (Figure 2—figure supplement 2).
claims.evidence: This is inferred from the observation that o-Tyr does not inhibit growth and is not used by PheRS.

claims.claim: E. coli lacking PheRS editing activity showed a reduction in growth relative to wild type when grown in media where ROS exposure increased.
claims.source: E. coli lacking PheRS editing activity showed a reduction in growth relative to wild type when grown in media where ROS exposure increased, consistent with the accumulation of free m-Tyr and its subsequent utilization in protein synthesis (Figure 7B).
claims.evidence: This is demonstrated by growth assays under oxidative stress shown in Figure 7B.

claims.claim: PheRS editing activity affords E. coli protection against the co-translational insertion of non-proteinogenic amino acids that accumulate during oxidative stress.
claims.source: Taken together, our data indicate that PheRS editing activity affords E. coli protection against the co-translational insertion of non-proteinogenic amino acids that accumulate during oxidative stress.
claims.evidence: This is inferred from the combined observations of m-Tyr accumulation under oxidative stress and growth defects in editing-deficient strains.

claims.claim: The fidelity of aminoacyl-tRNA synthetases needs to be at or above 1 in 3,000, which is cited as an approximate overall level of error for protein synthesis.
claims.source: It has long been proposed that the fidelity of aminoacyl-tRNA synthetases needs to be at or above 1 in 3,000, which is cited as an approximate overall level of error for protein synthesis (Loftfield and Vanderjagt, 1972).
claims.evidence: This is supported by citation to a classic study on translation fidelity.

claims.claim: Protection against both p-Tyr and m-Tyr incorporation at Phe codons appears critical in E. coli.
claims.source: Protection against both p-Tyr and m-Tyr incorporation at Phe codons appears critical in E. coli as the PheRS enzyme maintains high active-site selectivity against p-Tyr as well as post–transfer editing activity against m-Tyr-tRNAPhe.
claims.evidence: This is inferred from the combined observations of high specificity and editing activity.

claims.claim: E. coli PheRS requires editing activity to protect the proteome from toxic effects of the non-proteinogenic amino acid m-Tyr.
claims.source: E. coli PheRS requires this editing activity to protect the proteome from toxic effects of the non-proteinogenic amino acid m-Tyr, which is poorly discriminated against by the active site of the enzyme.
claims.evidence: This is demonstrated by the growth defects and m-Tyr incorporation in editing-deficient strains.

claims.claim: m-Tyr is poorly discriminated against by the active site of E. coli PheRS.
claims.source: E. coli PheRS requires this editing activity to protect the proteome from toxic effects of the non-proteinogenic amino acid m-Tyr, which is poorly discriminated against by the active site of the enzyme.
claims.evidence: This is demonstrated by kinetic data showing relatively efficient activation of m-Tyr.

claims.claim: Ala294 is primarily responsible for specificity against binding of para-substituted Phe analogs in E. coli PheRS.
claims.source: Ala294 is primarily responsible for specificity against binding of para-substituted Phe analogs, while Gln174 and Glu210 help stabilize the hydroxyl of non-cognate m-Tyr at position 3 of the ring (E. coli numbering) (Klipcan et al., 2009).
claims.evidence: This is supported by citation to structural studies.

claims.claim: Gln174 and Glu210 help stabilize the hydroxyl of non-cognate m-Tyr at position 3 of the ring in E. coli PheRS.
claims.source: Ala294 is primarily responsible for specificity against binding of para-substituted Phe analogs, while Gln174 and Glu210 help stabilize the hydroxyl of non-cognate m-Tyr at position 3 of the ring (E. coli numbering) (Klipcan et al., 2009).
claims.evidence: This is supported by citation to structural studies.

claims.claim: Glu210 is needed to hydrogen bond with the Phe amino group, ensuring correct orientation of the substrate for activation in E. coli PheRS.
claims.source: In the case of the cognate Phe substrate, Glu210 is also needed to hydrogen bond with the Phe amino group, ensuring correct orientation of the substrate for activation (Safro et al., 2005; Mermershtain et al., 2011).
claims.evidence: This is supported by citations to structural studies.

claims.claim: It is unlikely E. coli PheRS can select against recognition of m-Tyr while still maintaining efficient activity for the cognate amino acid.
claims.source: It is unlikely this enzyme selects against recognition of m-Tyr while still maintaining efficient activity for the cognate amino acid, therefore the maintenance of post–transfer editing activity is critical for fidelity in E. coli.
claims.evidence: This is inferred from structural and kinetic considerations.

claims.claim: The maintenance of post-transfer editing activity is critical for fidelity in E. coli.
claims.source: It is unlikely this enzyme selects against recognition of m-Tyr while still maintaining efficient activity for the cognate amino acid, therefore the maintenance of post–transfer editing activity is critical for fidelity in E. coli.
claims.evidence: This is inferred from the inability to discriminate against m-Tyr at the active site.

claims.claim: In eukaryotes, cytoplasmic PheRS editing is needed to protect the proteome from p-Tyr misincorporation.
claims.source: In eukaryotes, cytoplasmic PheRS editing is needed to protect the proteome from p-Tyr misincorporation. This finding concurs with the low Phe/p-Tyr specificity of the yeast cytoplasmic enzyme (Reynolds et al., 2010).
claims.evidence: This is demonstrated by the p-Tyr sensitivity of editing-deficient yeast strains.

claims.claim: The yeast strain encoding wild type ctPheRS is sensitive to high concentrations of m-Tyr.
claims.source: It is unclear if protection from m-Tyr incorporation is achieved through editing as the yeast strain encoding wild type ctPheRS is sensitive to high concentrations of m-Tyr
claims.evidence: This is demonstrated by growth assays showing m-Tyr sensitivity in wild-type yeast.

claims.claim: Naturally occurring non-proteinogenic amino acids occur widely in nature and are well-characterized by-products and/or intermediates of biosynthetic pathways.
claims.source: Naturally occurring non-proteinogenic amino acids occur widely in nature and are well-characterized by-products and/or intermediates of biosynthetic pathways (Richmond, 1962).
claims.evidence: This is supported by citation to a review on non-proteinogenic amino acids.

claims.claim: The non-proteinogenic amino acid m-Tyr has been detected in several eukaryotic proteomes.
claims.source: The non-proteinogenic amino acid m-Tyr has been detected in several eukaryotic proteomes and is one of the products of canonical aromatic amino acid oxidation (Wells-Knecht et al., 1993; Pennathur et al., 2001).
claims.evidence: This is supported by citations to studies detecting m-Tyr in proteomes.

claims.claim: m-Tyr is one of the products of canonical aromatic amino acid oxidation.
claims.source: The non-proteinogenic amino acid m-Tyr has been detected in several eukaryotic proteomes and is one of the products of canonical aromatic amino acid oxidation (Wells-Knecht et al., 1993; Pennathur et al., 2001).
claims.evidence: This is supported by citations to studies on oxidative damage.

claims.claim: The presence of hydroxylated forms of tyrosine in proteomes has previously been attributed to post-translational damage to proteins by hydroxyl radical species.
claims.source: The presence of hydroxylated forms of tyrosine in proteomes has previously been attributed to post-translational damage to proteins by hydroxyl radical species, and is often used as a marker for tissue damage due to the oxidative conditions of aging and disease.
claims.evidence: This is based on established knowledge in the field of oxidative stress.

claims.claim: m-Tyr and other Tyr analogs are substrates for translation in some organisms and could potentially be incorporated directly during protein synthesis.
claims.source: It has also been shown that m-Tyr and other Tyr analogs, for example L-DOPA, are substrates for translation in some organisms and could potentially be incorporated directly during protein synthesis (Rodgers et al., 2002; Ozawa et al., 2005; Gurer-Orhan et al., 2006; Klipcan et al., 2009; Moor et al., 2011).
claims.evidence: This is supported by multiple citations to studies on non-proteinogenic amino acid incorporation.

claims.claim: Incorporation of m-Tyr into the proteome of E. coli at Phe codons is toxic to the cell.
claims.source: Incorporation of m-Tyr into the proteome of E. coli at Phe codons is toxic to the cell, and in the absence of PheRS quality control this non-proteinogenic amino acid serves as an efficient substrate for translation.
claims.evidence: This is demonstrated by growth inhibition and m-Tyr incorporation data.

claims.claim: In the absence of PheRS quality control, m-Tyr serves as an efficient substrate for translation in E. coli.
claims.source: Incorporation of m-Tyr into the proteome of E. coli at Phe codons is toxic to the cell, and in the absence of PheRS quality control this non-proteinogenic amino acid serves as an efficient substrate for translation.
claims.evidence: This is demonstrated by aminoacylation and dipeptide synthesis assays.

claims.claim: α-aminobutyrate in the absence of ValRS editing is toxic at high concentrations.
claims.source: Other non-proteinogenic amino acids have also been shown to be potential threats to translation, such as α-aminobutyrate, which in the absence of ValRS editing is toxic at high concentrations, although the physiological conditions under which this non-protein amino acid might naturally accumulate to significant levels are unclear (Nangle et al., 2002).
claims.evidence: This is supported by citation to a study on ValRS editing.

claims.claim: The presence of m-Tyr in the proteome of wild type E. coli suggests misincorporation can also occur at Tyr codons but without cytotoxic sequelae.
claims.source: In contrast, the presence of m-Tyr in the proteome of wild type E. coli suggests misincorporation can also occur at Tyr codons but without cytotoxic sequelae.
claims.evidence: This is inferred from the detection of m-Tyr in wild-type proteomes and the lack of growth defects.

claims.claim: The cellular effects of non-proteinogenic amino acid incorporation are codon-dependent.
claims.source: These findings suggest that the cellular effects of non-proteinogenic amino acid incorporation are codon-dependent.
claims.evidence: This is inferred from the differential toxicity of m-Tyr at Phe vs Tyr codons.

claims.claim: Misincorporation of m-Tyr at Phe codons in the absence of PheRS quality control occurred at a frequency of 1% and had a significant impact on cellular viability and restricted growth.
claims.source: In E. coli, misincorporation of m-Tyr at Phe codons in the absence of PheRS quality control occurred at a frequency of 1% and had a significant impact on cellular viability and restricted growth.
claims.evidence: This is demonstrated by LC-MS/MS-MRM quantification and growth assays.

claims.claim: Misincorporation of canonical amino acids has been shown to be tolerated at rates of up to 10% without inhibiting growth.
claims.source: This contrasts with the effects of misincorporation of canonical amino acids, which have been shown to be tolerated at rates of up to 10% without inhibiting growth (Ruan et al., 2008).

results.result: PheRS editing is dispensable for E. coli and S. cerevisiae growth under standard laboratory conditions. Both E. coli pheT(G318W) and yeast frs1-1(D243A) editing-deficient strains showed no growth defects compared to wild-type under normal conditions, and phenotypic microarrays revealed no significant changes across 1920 growth conditions.
results.evaluation: Claims C27-C32 demonstrate through multiple experimental approaches (editing assays, growth curves, phenotypic microarrays) that PheRS editing is not required for viability under standard laboratory conditions in both E. coli and yeast. The data consistently show that editing-deficient strains grow normally when not challenged with specific stressors.

results.result: E. coli PheRS editing is not required for protection against p-Tyr toxicity. Elevated concentrations of p-Tyr (>3 mM) did not affect growth of editing-deficient strains, intracellular amino acid pools were similar between strains, and p-Tyr was not significantly misincorporated at Phe codons even in the absence of editing.
results.evaluation: Claims C33-C35, C57-C58 provide converging evidence from growth assays, amino acid pool measurements, and LC-MS/MS-MRM proteome analysis showing that p-Tyr does not pose a threat to E. coli even without PheRS editing. This is consistent with the high active-site specificity of E. coli PheRS against p-Tyr.

results.result: E. coli PheRS editing is essential for protection against m-Tyr toxicity. Growth of editing-deficient strains was inhibited in the presence of elevated m-Tyr, and this effect was observed in multiple strain backgrounds (NP37 and MG1655). In vitro editing assays confirmed that the G318W mutation ablates m-Tyr-tRNAPhe editing.
results.evaluation: Claims C36-C39 demonstrate through growth assays in multiple genetic backgrounds and in vitro editing assays that PheRS editing is specifically required to clear m-Tyr-tRNAPhe. The consistency across different strain backgrounds strengthens the conclusion that this is a general requirement in E. coli.

results.result: Neither o-Tyr nor L-DOPA are substrates for E. coli PheRS or pose threats to translation fidelity. Growth assays showed no inhibition with these amino acids, and aminoacylation assays confirmed that G318W PheRS cannot utilize o-Tyr or L-DOPA for tRNAPhe charging.
results.evaluation: Claims C40, C45, C100 provide consistent evidence from both growth and biochemical assays that o-Tyr and L-DOPA are not recognized by PheRS and therefore do not threaten translation fidelity. This demonstrates the specificity of PheRS discrimination among different tyrosine isomers.

results.result: Yeast PheRS editing provides limited protection from m-Tyr but is essential for protection against p-Tyr. The editing-deficient frs1-1(D243A) strain showed pronounced defects in p-Tyr resistance, while both wild-type and editing-deficient strains were comparably inhibited by m-Tyr.
results.evaluation: Claims C41-C42, C24-C25 demonstrate through yeast growth assays that the role of PheRS editing differs between organisms. The data clearly show that yeast editing is optimized for p-Tyr rather than m-Tyr protection, contrasting with the E. coli system.

results.result: E. coli PheRS poorly discriminates against m-Tyr at the active site but effectively discriminates against p-Tyr. Wild-type EcPheRS did not stably charge tRNAPhe with either isomer, but G318W utilized both, with m-Tyr being more efficient. Kinetic analysis showed m-Tyr is activated only 35-fold less efficiently than Phe, while p-Tyr is activated 3000-fold less efficiently.
results.evaluation: Claims C43-C44, C46-C47, C70 provide comprehensive kinetic and aminoacylation data demonstrating the differential specificity of E. coli PheRS against tyrosine isomers. The quantitative measurements support the conclusion that m-Tyr is poorly discriminated at the active site, necessitating editing.

results.result: Yeast PheRS enzymes efficiently utilize m-Tyr for aminoacylation but have different editing preferences. Wild-type ScctPheRS efficiently charges tRNAPhe with m-Tyr (71-fold lower kcat/KM than Phe) and preferentially edits p-Tyr-tRNAPhe over m-Tyr-tRNAPhe. ScmtPheRS also synthesizes m-Tyr-tRNAPhe more efficiently than p-Tyr-tRNAPhe.
results.evaluation: Claims C48-C51 provide kinetic and aminoacylation data showing that yeast PheRS enzymes have evolved different substrate specificities and editing preferences compared to E. coli. The data consistently demonstrate poor discrimination against m-Tyr at the active site and preferential editing of p-Tyr.

results.result: E. coli ribosomes do not discriminate against m-Tyr-tRNAPhe during translation. In vitro dipeptide synthesis assays showed similar levels of fMet-m-Tyr and fMet-Phe formation when m-Tyr-tRNAPhe was used to decode Phe codons.
results.evaluation: Claims C52-C53 demonstrate through in vitro translation assays that once m-Tyr-tRNAPhe is formed, it is efficiently used by ribosomes. This supports the conclusion that PheRS editing is the critical quality control checkpoint for preventing m-Tyr incorporation.

results.result: PheRS editing prevents misincorporation of m-Tyr at Phe codons in E. coli proteomes. LC-MS/MS-MRM analysis showed that the m-Tyr/Phe ratio increased from 0.015 in wild-type to 0.025 in editing-deficient strains, representing approximately 1% misincorporation at Phe codons, which significantly impacted cellular viability.
results.evaluation: Claims C54-C56, C88 provide direct proteomic evidence that PheRS editing protects against m-Tyr misincorporation. The quantitative LC-MS/MS-MRM data demonstrate measurable differences between wild-type and editing-deficient strains, linking biochemical activity to proteome composition and cellular phenotype.

results.result: E. coli TyrRS can aminoacylate tRNATyr with m-Tyr, potentially providing an alternative route for m-Tyr incorporation. The presence of m-Tyr in wild-type E. coli proteomes suggests misincorporation can occur at Tyr codons without cytotoxic effects.
results.evaluation: Claims C59-C60, C86 suggest an alternative pathway for m-Tyr incorporation via TyrRS, but the evidence is limited to in vitro aminoacylation assays (C59) and inference from proteome analysis (C86). The physiological relevance and contribution of this pathway relative to contamination or post-translational modification is unclear. Additional experiments would be needed to definitively establish TyrRS-mediated m-Tyr incorporation at Tyr codons.

results.result: Oxidative stress via ROS treatment leads to accumulation of m-Tyr and o-Tyr in E. coli intracellular amino acid pools. LC-MS/MS-MRM analysis showed that both isomers accumulate under conditions promoting hydroxyl radical formation, with o-Tyr being the more abundant product.
results.evaluation: Claims C62-C63, C98-C99 provide direct analytical evidence from LC-MS/MS-MRM showing accumulation of hydroxylated phenylalanine products under oxidative stress. The data clearly demonstrate that ROS treatment generates these non-proteinogenic amino acids in vivo.

results.result: PheRS editing is essential for E. coli growth and survival under oxidative stress conditions. Editing-deficient strains showed reduced growth when ROS exposure increased, consistent with m-Tyr accumulation and subsequent utilization in protein synthesis.
results.evaluation: Claims C65-C66, C23 demonstrate through growth assays under oxidative stress that PheRS editing provides protection under physiologically relevant stress conditions. This establishes the biological significance of editing activity beyond artificial amino acid supplementation experiments.

results.result: E. coli PheRS has evolved to discriminate against different Tyr isomers using a combination of substrate specificity (o-Tyr, p-Tyr) and editing activity (m-Tyr, p-Tyr). o-Tyr does not pose a threat to translation fidelity as it is not a substrate for PheRS.
results.evaluation: Claims C64, C101 synthesize the biochemical and growth data to show how E. coli PheRS employs complementary mechanisms for quality control. The inference is well-supported by the comprehensive characterization of PheRS specificity and editing against all three tyrosine isomers.

results.result: Yeast cytoplasmic PheRS has evolved specifically to discriminate against p-Tyr by editing, reflecting different evolutionary pressures compared to E. coli. This editing is needed to protect the proteome from p-Tyr misincorporation.
results.evaluation: Claims C102, C76 are supported by the combined yeast growth, kinetic, and editing data showing that yeast PheRS has low Phe/p-Tyr specificity but robust p-Tyr editing. This contrasts with E. coli and demonstrates organism-specific evolution of quality control mechanisms.

results.result: Structural features of E. coli PheRS active site explain its inability to discriminate against m-Tyr. Ala294 provides specificity against para-substituted analogs, while Gln174 and Glu210 stabilize m-Tyr. Glu210 is also required for cognate Phe binding, making it unlikely the enzyme can select against m-Tyr while maintaining activity for Phe.
results.evaluation: Claims C71-C75 provide structural rationalization for the biochemical observations, supported by citations to structural studies. The logic connecting active site architecture to substrate specificity and the necessity of editing is sound and consistent with the kinetic data.

results.result: The cellular effects of non-proteinogenic amino acid incorporation are codon-dependent, and non-proteinogenic amino acids present a greater challenge than canonical amino acid misincorporation. m-Tyr misincorporation at 1% at Phe codons caused significant toxicity, while canonical amino acid misincorporation is tolerated at rates up to 10%.
results.evaluation: Claims C87, C89-C90 synthesize the findings to draw broader conclusions about translation quality control. The comparison to canonical amino acid misincorporation (C89, supported by citation) provides important context for the significance of the 1% m-Tyr misincorporation observed.

results.result: Many 'dispensable' editing functions may actually be essential for growth under conditions that lead to accumulation of potentially toxic levels of non-proteinogenic amino acids.
results.evaluation: Claim C91 represents a well-supported generalization from the specific findings. The demonstration that editing is dispensable under standard conditions but essential under oxidative stress or amino acid challenge directly supports this broader conclusion about the conditional essentiality of editing functions.

results.result: Background claims establishing the general principles of aminoacyl-tRNA synthetase function, editing mechanisms, conservation patterns, and the biochemistry of oxidative damage to amino acids.
results.evaluation: These claims (C1, C4-C21, C67, C78-C82, C85, C92-C93, C95-C97) represent established knowledge supported by citations to prior literature and general biochemical principles. They provide necessary context for interpreting the novel findings but are not themselves novel results of this study.

results.result: Bacterial PheRS efficiently edits m-Tyr-tRNAPhe, and this editing activity is essential for cellular growth and survival under cytotoxic amino acid and oxidative stress conditions. m-Tyr produced through oxidative damage is a significant threat to translation accuracy in E. coli.
results.evaluation: Claims C22, C2-C3 represent the central thesis of the manuscript, supported by the comprehensive set of biochemical, growth, and proteomic experiments described in the other claim groups. The evidence consistently demonstrates both the editing activity and its physiological necessity.

results.result: Protection against both p-Tyr and m-Tyr incorporation at Phe codons is critical in E. coli. E. coli PheRS maintains high active-site selectivity against p-Tyr and editing activity against m-Tyr. Incorporation of m-Tyr at Phe codons is toxic, and m-Tyr serves as an efficient substrate for translation in the absence of editing.
results.evaluation: Claims C68-C69, C83-C84 synthesize the biochemical and cellular data to explain the dual quality control strategy of E. coli PheRS. The evidence from kinetics, editing assays, growth experiments, and proteomics consistently supports these conclusions.

results.result: Wild-type yeast encoding functional ctPheRS editing is sensitive to high concentrations of m-Tyr.
results.evaluation: Claim C77 is directly supported by the growth assay data in Figure 3B showing that wild-type yeast exhibits growth inhibition at high m-Tyr concentrations. This demonstrates that yeast PheRS editing does not provide effective protection against m-Tyr.

results.result: The G318W mutation in E. coli PheRS reduces posttransfer editing activity by more than 70-fold in vitro.
results.evaluation: Claim C26 is supported by citations to previous biochemical studies (Roy et al., 2004; Ling et al., 2007a) that characterized this mutation. This provides the rationale for using this mutation to create editing-deficient strains.

results.result: ROS generated via the Fenton reaction can catalyze conversion of Phe to m-Tyr, and the formation of intracellular m-Tyr in E. coli under physiological conditions is possibly a result of cellular exposure to H2O2.
results.evaluation: Claim C61 is supported by citations to studies on oxidative damage. Claim C94 is a reasonable speculation based on known chemistry and the experimental demonstration that ROS treatment generates m-Tyr (C62). Together these establish the physiological relevance of m-Tyr formation.
